The report we present today reflects the devastating impact of these activities on the people of Iran and presents our findings on the suppression of the 2025-2026 protests, the continuing hostilities, and the ongoing repressive acts by the government of Iran. It consolidates our findings to date on violations of international human rights law, international humanitarian law, and on crimes under international law. Our report draws upon interviews conducted with 73 witnesses, Satellite imagery, video and photographic material and information from experts, we've also examined 75 documents received from the government of Iran since the 1st of January this year. Our investigations have been held despite encountering serious operational constraints, including continuing lack of access to the country, the government of Iran's communication restrictions, and their new and increased repressive measures, which have exacerbated the fear of reprisals and prevented victims and witnesses from coming forward in greater numbers. The hostilities have further severely disrupted access to information. The present findings should be understood, therefore, as capturing only part of the scale and extent of violations and crimes. Further investigation is needed. As you'll be aware, we've just marked the fourth anniversary of the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in custody and the ensuing women life freedom protests, which were triggered in 2022. That had triggered large scale repression, resulting in gross human rights violations, some of which the mission found amounted to crimes against humanity by the government of Iran. Four years on, there has been no accountability, with repressive laws and practices remaining entrenched. Once again, on the 28th of December 2025, people took to the streets across the country, first in reaction to mounting economic grievances, and then in calls for political change. A massive mobilization by people across the country was met with an extraordinarily brutal response by the Iranian authorities. The scale and breadth of this response have left Iranian people in agony and shock. The government's response marked a clear and extreme escalation in their use of lethal force and of mass arrests, with the 8th and 9th of January this year being the deadliest period. Security forces used lethal force to kill and injure protesters and bystanders, including children, although none of them posed an imminent threat of death or serious injury. Protesters sustained severe wounds to the head, the chest, and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness in many cases. Security forces also used less lethal weapons and ammunition outside of less lethal parameters to kill or injure protesters. The government of Iran has itself published a list of 3,038 names of people killed. It is also reported that 25,000 people were injured, with more than 50% of them requiring surgery. These numbers are already staggeringly, horrifyingly high. However, we believe the actual numbers may be significantly higher and are continuing to investigate. With regard to boys and girls killed and injured in the context of the protests, it has been reported that at least 221 children were killed. Witnesses have reported child victims being shot, with the youngest now reported as having been only four and a half months old. Many of those injured were unable to access healthcare. Security forces present in and around healthcare facilities used unnecessary force against and detained injured protesters, their family members, and medical staff inside hospitals. The mission found that authorities carried out large-scale arrests and detention during the protests and in their aftermath. This included the arrests of children and summons just to lawyers representing protesters. Security and intelligence forces also tortured detainees and subjected them to ill treatment. Families suffered torments in trying to determine the fate and whereabouts of their loved ones. The mission also found that Iran intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters. Between March to 31st August this year, the government of Iran executed at least 29 men in connection with the protests, five of them publicly. More than 70 people, including at least five women and three boys, remain at imminent risk of being sentenced to death or executed in relation to the protests. Some of those sentenced or executed had been charged under the broadly and vaguely formulated 2025 Espionage Act. Death sentences and executions follow trials marked by violations of due process and fair trial guarantees, forced confessions, and the denial of access to lawyers of one's own choosing. These are all well-established patterns documented earlier by the mission, which continue in flagrant disregard of calls from UN human rights bodies and in violation of Iran's obligations under international human rights law. We were deeply perturbed by the unprecedented scale of the restrictions on digital space imposed during the protests and their aftermath, including the start of the hostilities, with the government imposing the longest nationwide internet shutdown on record from the 8th of January onwards for more than five months. This prevented victims from seeking help and families from locating loved ones. It also critically prevented documentation of the crackdown. Disruptions of digital communications deepened people's isolation inside Iran and from the outside world. The mission is gravely concerned by draft legislation now before the Iranian parliament that threatens to make this isolation worse. It proposes imprisonment of any person, including a journalist, an academic, or an activist for up to 30 years simply for "communicating" with "foreign persons and entities" from designated states. If enacted, this law would curtail freedom of expression further, including to share and receive information and possible cooperation with UN human rights bodies. The Iranian government's repression of the recent protests has led the mission to find Iran responsible for gross human rights violations, many of which amount to the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment, and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts. Mr. President, Excellencies, The Mission's mandate requires us to investigate and report on any human rights violations committed in Iran. To reflect the totality of the violations to which people in Iran have been subjected during this period, I will now speak about two emblematic incidents in relation to the ongoing hostilities. The first incident is the US airstrike on Shajareh Tayyebey Primary School in Minab, Hormozgan Province, in southern Iran. This building, a readily identifiable primary school, was struck by two cruise missiles, resulting, we have found, in 157 people killed, including 123 boys and girls, according to credible sources. We found reasonable grounds to believe that the airstrike conducted by the United States amounted to the war crime of making a civilian object the object of an attack. The second incident is another US airstrike against a sports center in a residential area of Lamed in Fars province. Local authorities determined that this airstrike killed 22 people, including 10 women and 12 men. We found reasonable grounds to believe that this US airstrike amounted to the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack, resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects. We are gravely concerned by the repeated airstrikes and threats of airstrikes on Iran, which continue to put civilians' lives at risk and exacerbate civilian suffering by destroying homes and livelihoods and disrupting access to basic services, including education and health. We are also alarmed by reports of Iranian strikes in the region that have struck residential buildings, civilian airports, and other civilian infrastructure, injuring and killing civilians, including migrant workers. The Mission is also concerned about the reported impact of the ongoing hostilities and recently imposed unilateral sectoral sanctions on deteriorating living conditions and sharply rising prices for basic goods inside the country, severely impacting the enjoyment of people to their rights to education, health, and adequate food and housing. Excellencies, the sufferings of people in Iran, rooted in intensified repression and violence by their government, the continuing hostilities, and growing economic hardship, compounded by unilateral sexual sanctions, must come to an end. First, we call on the government of Iran to cease all human rights violations and crimes against humanity. It must immediately halt executions, release all individuals arbitrarily detained, promptly withdraw the Countering Foreign Infiltration Bill and repeal the Espionage Act, and undertake effective, independent, and impartial investigations into these violations and crimes. Iran must ensure accountability, provide reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence, including structural reforms. Further, considering the reservations many victims have expressed on the prospects of effective justice and accountability within Iran, we call on member states to pursue third state accountability for such violations and crimes through universal jurisdiction, while ensuring emergency support to victims. Secondly, we call on the parties to the conflict to immediately cease hostilities and on all member states to take urgent diplomatic action to this end. Thirdly, we call on all parties to the conflict to conduct prompt, independent and impartial investigations into allegations of violations of international humanitarian law, including on the US with respect to the findings made by the mission, and to ensure accountability, guarantees of non-reparation and reparations for victims and their families. I thank you.
